clue.text: Go west presumably? Absolutely

parts.note: to go is to quit, leave
anyone heading west is presumably leaving the east, E on the compass, so this phrase supplies what is left

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether heading west is the plan and gets an emphatic yes.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is built backwards: quitting E (east) presumably means going west. 'Go west' also suggests dying, a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words express complete agreement or totality, as in 'quite right' meaning entirely right.

clue.text: Living tree producing calcium oxide

parts.note: quick is an old word for living, as in the quick and the dead
the lime is a tree, the linden

explanation.surface: A living tree is somehow manufacturing a chemical compound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quick' meaning alive survives in 'the quick and the dead'.
explanation.definitionFit: The white caustic solid made by burning limestone is the chemist's CaO.

clue.text: Florida hotel's in a state? Quite the opposite

indicators.note: in, with Quite the opposite turning it round, says the state sits inside the words Florida hotel

parts.note: the run is read across the two words

explanation.surface: A Florida hotel is in some state of disorder, or so it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue says the hotel is in a state; 'Quite the opposite' flips it: the state is in 'Florida hotel', running from fl-OR-IDA into HO-tel.
explanation.definitionFit: Idaho is one of the fifty United States, in the north-west.

clue.text: Being, in the wrong scene, exit

indicators.note: in the wrong order means the letters must be put right by rearranging

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Life, with an actor exiting in the wrong scene, is a stage mishap.
explanation.definitionFit: Being, as a noun, is the state of living or having reality.

clue.text: Bat's also rum out for a very low score

indicators.note: out signals that the letters are put out of their order and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the possessive s counted as a letter
a misprint for run; R is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a run

explanation.surface: A batsman's companion is also run out, leaving a dismal total.
explanation.walkthrough: The paper prints 'rum', but the wordplay needs 'run', R in cricket. 'out' rearranges BATSALSO plus R. In golf an albatross is three under par on a hole, a very low score.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf this term names a hole completed three strokes under par, an exceptionally low tally.

clue.text: Shellfish a nonsense? Say why not

indicators.note: not means the following sound is left out of the word

parts.note: baloney is slang for nonsense

indicators.note: say means the word why is spoken, giving the sound of a letter

parts.note: said aloud, these words sound like Y

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses shellfish as rubbish and asks why not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say why' gives Y, the letter that sounds like 'why'; 'not' removes it from A BALONEY.
explanation.definitionFit: The abalone is a sea snail, an edible marine mollusc with a pearly ear-shaped shell.

clue.text: Laurel, note, may be a killer

parts.note: the bay is the laurel tree

indicators.note: may be signals the letters could be some other arrangement

explanation.surface: Laurel wreaths and a note may count as deadly weapons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be' rearranges NOTE into ONET.
explanation.definitionFit: A blade fixed to a rifle's muzzle is a lethal weapon, a killing instrument.

clue.text: Control position for loom

definitions.meaning: the control ... at an airfield directs traffic
to loom is to rise high above

explanation.surface: Where a weaving machine is operated from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loom' looks like the weaving frame, but it is the verb: to rise up threateningly.
explanation.definitionFit: An airport's control centre is a tall building, and to rise over things is to tower.

clue.text: It takes a charade to disguise such solid figures

indicators.note: to disguise is to change the look, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Playing a guessing game is needed to hide certain geometric shapes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charade' suggests the parlour game, but it just supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Octahedra are solids with eight faces, like two square pyramids base to base.

clue.text: Not much of a fight

explanation.surface: A brawl that hardly amounted to anything.
explanation.definitionFit: A morsel or fragment is not much, and a scuffle or brawl is a fight.

clue.text: Fancied the single girl holding a drink

parts.note: single means one, written as the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: holding means the girl's name wraps around the other letters

parts.note: Mary is a girl's name
gin is a spirit, a drink

explanation.surface: A man imagined that an unattached woman was clutching a glass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancied' looks like 'took a liking to' but is an adjective here: dreamed up. 'Single' as I is the Roman numeral one.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fancied in the sense of conjured up by the mind is unreal, existing only in thought.

clue.text: "Too much of _ hast thou, poor Ophelia" (Hamlet)

definitions.text: "Too much of _ hast thou, poor Ophelia" (Hamlet)

parts.words: Too much of _ hast thou, poor Ophelia
parts.note: Laertes speaks this line in Hamlet after his sister has drowned; the gap is the element that killed her

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: Ophelia drowned in a brook, so Laertes says she has had too much of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ophelia drowned in a brook, so the substance she had too much of is the liquid of rivers and seas.

clue.text: A blow from this is nothing to a Yorkshireman

definitions.text: A blow from this is nothing to a Yorkshireman

parts.words: A blow from this is nothing to a Yorkshireman
parts.note: the Russian whip in question is pronounced like the Yorkshire dialect word nowt, meaning nothing

explanation.walkthrough: Yorkshire dialect says 'nowt' for nothing, and the whip's name can be said the same way, so its blow is literally 'nothing' to a Yorkshireman.
explanation.definitionFit: A Russian scourge or lash once used for flogging criminals.

clue.text: Having to admit the cockney girl's a tramp, perhaps

parts.note: to own up is to admit
a cockney drops the h, so her becomes 'er, the girl
a tramp steamer is a ship with no fixed route, so a tramp is an example of a ship

explanation.surface: Someone is made to concede that a London woman is a vagrant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tramp' suggests a vagrant, but a tramp is a cargo ship working no fixed route; 'perhaps' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Having something means possessing it, the state of being its proprietor.

clue.text: Young English prince of the royal blood? No

parts.note: a young child is an infant

explanation.surface: Is the boy an English royal prince? No, he is not.
explanation.walkthrough: The closing 'No' warns that the prince is not English: the title belongs to a younger son of the Spanish or Portuguese king.
explanation.definitionFit: In Spain and Portugal the title is given to a king's son who is not heir to the throne.

clue.text: Archduke could have been 13's father

definitions.meaning: the Habsburg heir shot at Sarajevo in 1914, whose murder set off the First World War
Spanish kings of this name fathered princes bearing the title at 13

explanation.surface: An archduke might have sired a Spanish prince.
explanation.walkthrough: 13 is the across answer naming a Spanish prince; several kings of Spain bore this name.
explanation.definitionFit: The archduke assassinated in 1914 bore the name, as did kings of Aragon and Spain, fathers of royal princes.

clue.text: Act, by Jove, to end Ruth's discomfiture

indicators.note: discomfiture is upset and confusion, so these letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, the possessive s not counted

explanation.surface: A dramatic gesture, exclaimed with surprise, is meant to stop Ruth's embarrassment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by Jove' reads as a mild oath, but here Jove is Jupiter, whose act is to hurl thunderbolts.
explanation.definitionFit: Jupiter, the Roman sky god, was famed for wielding thunderbolts and rumbling storms.

clue.text: Northern Irelander needs a coat on the island

indicators.note: on means the first piece sits on top of the second in this down answer

parts.note: an ulster is a long heavy overcoat
the Isle of Man is the island in the Irish Sea

explanation.surface: A man from the north of Ireland needs warm clothing when visiting the island.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan prints Irelander. Ulster is the northern province of Ireland, and the Isle of Man lies in the Irish Sea; 'on' stacks the coat above the island in this down light.
explanation.definitionFit: Ulster is the northern province of Ireland, so its native is from the north of the island.

clue.text: Angry note dispatched — not completely satisfied

parts.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale
something dispatched has been sent

indicators.note: not completely means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: after a meal one is full, satisfied

explanation.surface: An irate message was posted, its writer still unhappy.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling bitter indignation at being treated unfairly is a form of anger.

clue.text: Hemingway includes a pledge

indicators.note: includes means the novelist's first name takes a letter inside it

parts.note: Ernest Hemingway was the American novelist

explanation.surface: The novelist Hemingway features a solemn promise in his work.
explanation.definitionFit: An earnest is money paid as a token or guarantee, a pledge of good faith.

clue.text: Toys with sweets

definitions.meaning: British desserts of sponge, fruit, custard and cream

explanation.surface: Playthings handed out with sweets.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a trifle is a layered pudding and 'sweets' can mean puddings; to toy with something is to trifle with it.
explanation.definitionFit: To toy is to treat idly, and the layered British puddings are sweet dishes.

clue.text: Corinthian team in informal clothes

definitions.meaning: Corinthian-... is an old amateur English football club
relaxed everyday garments as opposed to formal wear

explanation.surface: A football side turns out in relaxed gear.
explanation.walkthrough: Corinthian-Casuals is a famous amateur football club from south London.
explanation.definitionFit: The football club's second name doubles as the word for leisure wear like jeans and sweaters.

clue.text: "With — tread, Upon our prey we steal" (Gilbert)

definitions.text: "With — tread, Upon our prey we steal" (Gilbert)

parts.words: With — tread, Upon our prey we steal
parts.note: the pirates' chorus in The Pirates of Penzance creeps in softly like a stalking feline

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation from Gilbert and Sullivan's The Pirates of Penzance.
explanation.definitionFit: Stealthy and silent like a cat stalking prey.

clue.text: Turn some snow to spray

parts.note: to turn round is to spin
a drift is a bank of snow piled by the wind

explanation.surface: A gust turns part of a snowfall into a fine shower.
explanation.definitionFit: Spindrift is sea spray or fine snow blown off the crests of waves or ridges.

clue.text: Colour of a mollusc

definitions.meaning: the cuttlefish, whose genus name is this word

explanation.surface: The shade of a shellfish.
explanation.definitionFit: The brown pigment comes from cuttlefish ink, and the cuttlefish genus carries the same name.

clue.text: One who is stupid but may be capped

definitions.text: One who is stupid but may be capped

parts.words: One who is stupid but may be capped
parts.note: capped suggests a sporting honour but refers to the cone-shaped hat once put on a slow pupil

explanation.walkthrough: 'capped' suggests a sportsman honoured for his country, but it is the pointed hat once given to a slow pupil.
explanation.definitionFit: A slow learner, once made to wear a conical paper hat in class.

clue.text: Mischievous for the Spanish to end in Paris

parts.note: el is the Spanish for the
fin is French for end

explanation.surface: A playful remark about a Spaniard heading off to finish up in France.
explanation.definitionFit: Elves are impish, so an elfin manner is impishly playful.

clue.text: Waller receives a note from the Norms

indicators.note: receives means the jazzman's name takes a letter inside it

parts.note: Fats Waller was the American jazz pianist
E is one of the musical notes

explanation.surface: A jazz pianist gets a message from the Norse goddesses of destiny.
explanation.walkthrough: The Norns are the Norse goddesses of destiny, matching the three Fates of Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: Norse myth's three spinners of destiny correspond to the Greek trio who decide human lots.

clue.text: Pop right inside for fish

indicators.note: inside means one letter goes into the middle of another word

parts.note: to pop something is British slang for pawning it

explanation.surface: Dad goes right indoors to collect the fish supper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' suggests a father, but in British slang to pop is to pawn: hand goods to a pawnbroker for a loan. R goes inside PAWN.
explanation.definitionFit: A prawn is a shellfish, loosely counted as fish in a fishmonger's sense.

clue.text: Told to illuminate a certificate if it has a recurrent theme

indicators.note: told means the word is spoken and its sound written in a different spelling

parts.note: to light up is to illuminate
the MOT is the annual British roadworthiness certificate for a car
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is advised to light up a document if it keeps repeating itself.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the MOT is the yearly road-safety test certificate for cars. 'Told' turns LIGHT into its sound-alike LEIT.
explanation.definitionFit: A leitmotif, from Wagner's operas, is a musical phrase or idea that keeps returning through a work.

clue.text: One who's got it coming to him sees dread shape

definitions.text: One who's got it coming to him

indicators.note: to shape is to form anew, so these letters are given a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone due for punishment looks ahead with fear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got it coming to him' suggests deserved punishment; here it is just a letter being delivered.
explanation.definitionFit: The person a letter is directed to is the one the post is coming to.

clue.text: States girl may have this accent

definitions.text: States girl may have this accent

parts.words: States girl may have this accent
parts.note: an American woman's speech is stereotyped as a twang voiced through the nose

explanation.walkthrough: 'States' means the United States: an American accent is often called a twang produced through the nose.
explanation.definitionFit: A twang produced with air through the nose, a common caricature of American speech.
